source_text: Vanr autem et qui in aliena dicunt Deum venisse, velut aliena concupiscentem, uti eum hominem qui ab altero factus esset exhiberet ei Deo, qui neque fecisset neque condidisset, sed et ? qui desolatus esset ab initio a propria hominum fabricatione. Non justus adventus ejus qui secundum eos %adyenit in aliena; neque vere nos redemit sanguine suo, si non vere homo factus est, restaurans suo plasmati quod dictum est in principio, factum aliena in dolo diripiens, sed sua propria juste et benigne assuquantum attinet quidem ad apostasiam, juste suo sanguine redimens nos ab ea; quantum autem ad nos, qui redemti sumus, benigne. Nihil enim illi ante dedimus, neque desiderat aliquid a nobis, quasi indigens ; nos autem indigemus ejus que est ad eum communionis: et propterea benigne effudit semetipsum, ut nos colligeret in sinum Patris. * Vani autem omnimodo, qui universam dispositionem Dei contemnunt, et carnis salutem negant et regenerationem ejus spernunt, dicentes non eam capacem esse incorruptibilitatis. 4Si autem non salvetur heee nec Dominus sanguine suo redemit nos, neque calix Eucharistize communicatio sanguinis ejus est, neque panis quem frangimus communicatio corporis ejus est.* Sanguis enim non est nisi a venis et carnibus, et a reliqua quze est secundum hominem substantia, qua vere factum Verbum Dei, sanguine suo redemit nos. Quemadmodum et Apostolus ejus ait: In quo habemus redemtionem per sanguinem ejus, et remissionem peccaTpepouedar Tv de 2. Et quoniam membra ejus sumus, et per creaturam nutrimur; creaturam autem ipse nobis prestat, solem suum oriri faciens, et pluens quemadmodum vult, eum calicem qui est creatura, suum sanguinem qui effusus est, ex quo auget nostrum sanguinem ; et eum panem qui est a creatura, suum corpus confirmavit, ex quo nostra auget corpora. Quando ergo et mixtus calix, et factus panis percipit Verbum Dei, et fit Eucharistia sanguinis et corporis Christi, ex quibus augetur et consistit carnis nostree substantia ; quomodo carnem negant capacem esse donationis Dei, quee est vita eterna, quee sanguine et corpore Christi nutritur, et membrum ejus est? Quemadmodum et beatus A postolus ait in epistola que est ad Ephesios; Quoniam membra sumus corporis ejus, de carne ejus, et de ossibus ejus: non de spiritali aliquo et invisibili homine dicens heec; (Spiritus enim neque ossa, neque carnes habet) sed de ea dispositione, quee est secundum ? verum hominem, que ex carnibus et nervis et ossibus consistit ; quae de calice, qui est sanguis ejus, nutritur; et de pane, quod est corpus ejus, augetur. 3. Et quemadmodum lignum yitis depositum in terram, suo fructificat tempore, et granum tritici decidens in terram et dissolutum, multiplex surgit per Spiritum Dei, qui continet omnia ; quee deinde per sapientiam in usum ‘ hominis yeniunt, et percipientia verbum Dei Eucharistia fiunt, quod est corpus et sanguis Christi: sic et nostra corpora ex ea nutrita, et reposita in terram, et resoluta in ea, resurgent in suo tempore, Verbo Dei resurrectionem eis donante, in gloriam Dei Patris: qui huic mortali immortalitatem cireumdat, et corruptibili incorruptelam gratuito donat, quoniam virtus Dei in infirmitate perficitur: ut non quasi ex nobisipsis habentes vitam, inflemur aliquando et extollamur adversus Deum, ingratam mentem accipientes; experimento Tautem discentes, quoniam ex illius magnitudine, et non ex nostra habemus in zeternum perseverantiam, neque ab ea que est circa § Deum gloria, sicuti est, frustremur aliquando, neque nostram naturam ignoremus ; sed ut sciamus, et quid Deus potest, et quid homo beneficii accipit: et non erremus aliquando a vera comprehensione eorum qu sunt, et quemadmodum sunt, id est Dei et Et numquid forte, quaemadmodum preediximus, propter hoe passus est Deus fieri in nobis resolutionem; ut per omnia eruditi, in omnibus simus diligentes, neque Deum, neque nosmetipsos ignorantes ?
pass_a_gloss: But vain are those who say God came into something alien, as if into something alien He was desiring, so that He might show to God, who neither made nor founded, a man who had been made by another, and who was deserted from the beginning by the proper fabrication of men. Not just is the coming of the one who according to them came into something alien; nor did He truly redeem us with His blood, if He was not truly made man, restoring to His own creation what was said in the beginning, snatching away what was alien in deceit, but rather His own proper things justly and kindly restoring as far as it pertains to apostasy, justly redeeming us from it with His blood; as far as we are concerned, who have been redeemed, kindly. For we did not give anything to Him beforehand, nor does He desire anything from us, as if He were in need; but we are in need of what is communion with Him; and therefore He kindly poured out Himself, so that He might gather us into the bosom of the Father. But vain in every way are those who despise the entire disposition of God, and deny the salvation of the flesh, and scorn its regeneration, saying it is not capable of incorruptibility. For if this flesh is not saved, nor did the Lord redeem us with His blood, neither is the cup of the Eucharist the communication of His blood, nor is the bread which we break the communication of His body. For blood is not except from veins and flesh, and from the rest which is according to human substance, by which the Word of God, having been truly made, redeemed us with His blood. Just as His Apostle also says: In whom we have redemption through His blood, and remission of sins. And since we are His members, and are nourished through creation; and creation He Himself provides for us, making His sun rise, and raining as He wills, that cup which is creation, His blood which was poured out, from which our blood is increased; and that bread which is from creation, He confirmed His body, from which our bodies are increased. When, therefore, the mixed cup, and the made bread receive the Word of God, and become the Eucharist of the blood and body of Christ, from which the substance of our flesh is increased and consists; how do they deny that flesh is capable of receiving the gift of God, which is eternal life, which is nourished by the blood and body of Christ, and is a member of Him? Just as the blessed Apostle also says in the epistle which is to the Ephesians: Since we are members of His body, of His flesh, and of His bones; not saying these things of some spiritual and invisible man; (for the Spirit does not have bones or flesh) but of that disposition which is according to the true man, which consists of flesh, and nerves, and bones; which is nourished from the cup, which is His blood; and is increased from the bread, which is His body. And just as the wood of the vine, deposited in the earth, produces fruit in its time, and the grain of wheat, falling into the earth and dissolved, rises up multiple through the Spirit of God, who contains all things; which then, through wisdom, come into use for man, and receiving the Word of God become the Eucharist, which is the body and blood of Christ: so also our bodies, nourished from that, and deposited in the earth, and resolved into it, will rise again in their time, the Word of God giving them resurrection, in the glory of God the Father; who surrounds this mortal with immortality, and gives incorruptibility to the corruptible gratuitously; because the power of God is perfected in weakness: so that we, not having life from ourselves, may not at some time be puffed up against God, receiving an ungrateful mind; but rather, learning by experience, that we have perseverance from His greatness, and not from our own, and that we may not be deprived of the glory which is around God, as it is; and that we may not ignore our nature; but that we may know what God can do, and what man receives as a benefit; and that we may not err at some time from the true comprehension of those things which are, and how they are, that is, of God and of man. And did God perhaps suffer for this reason, that He might become resolution in us; so that, being instructed through all things, we may be diligent in all things, neither ignoring God nor ourselves?

pass_b_english: Those who claim that God came into something alien, as if desiring what is foreign, are empty in their thinking. They suppose He did this to present a man made by another to a God who neither made nor founded anything, a man abandoned from the beginning by the true fashioning of humanity. The coming of such a one is not just. Nor did He truly redeem us by His blood if He was not truly made man, restoring to His own creation what was declared in the beginning. He did not snatch away what was alien through deceit; rather, He justly and kindly restores what is properly His. As far as apostasy is concerned, He justly redeems us from it by His blood; as far as we who are redeemed are concerned, He acts kindly. We gave Him nothing beforehand, nor does He desire anything from us as though He were in need. We are the ones who need communion with Him, and so He kindly poured Himself out to gather us into the Father's bosom.

Those who despise God's entire economy, deny the salvation of the flesh, and scorn its regeneration, saying it is incapable of incorruptibility, are vain in every way. For if this flesh is not saved, then the Lord did not redeem us with His blood. Neither is the cup of the Eucharist a participation in His blood, nor is the bread we break a participation in His body (1 Cor 10:16). Blood comes only from veins and flesh, and from the rest of what belongs to human substance. By that very substance the Word of God was truly made flesh and redeemed us with His blood. His Apostle also says: "In Him we have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of sins" (Col 1:14). Since we are His members and are nourished through creation, He Himself provides that creation for us — making His sun rise and sending rain as He wills. The cup, which comes from creation, He made His own blood poured out, by which our blood is increased. The bread, which comes from creation, He confirmed as His own body, by which our bodies are increased. When the mixed cup and the baked bread receive the Word of God, they become the Eucharist of the blood and body of Christ, from which the substance of our flesh is increased and sustained. How then can they deny that flesh is capable of receiving God's gift, which is eternal life — flesh that is nourished by the blood and body of Christ and is a member of Him? The blessed Apostle says in the letter to the Ephesians: "We are members of His body, of His flesh and of His bones" (Eph 5:30). He does not say this of some spiritual, invisible man — for the Spirit has neither bones nor flesh — but of that constitution which belongs to the true human being, consisting of flesh, nerves, and bones. This constitution is nourished from the cup which is His blood, and increased from the bread which is His body.

Just as a vine shoot planted in the earth bears fruit in its season, and a grain of wheat falling into the earth, dissolved, rises multiplied by the Spirit of God who contains all things — and these then, through wisdom, come into human use, and receiving the Word of God become the Eucharist, which is the body and blood of Christ — so also our bodies, nourished by it, laid in the earth and dissolved there, will rise again in their season. The Word of God gives them resurrection, to the glory of God the Father, who clothes this mortal with immortality and freely gives incorruptibility to the corruptible. For God's power is perfected in weakness (2 Cor 12:9). This is so that we, not having life from ourselves, may not at some time be puffed up against God, harboring an ungrateful mind. Rather, learning by experience, we know that we have perseverance for eternity from His greatness, not our own. Thus we are not deprived of the glory that surrounds God as it truly is, nor do we ignore our own nature. Instead we come to know what God can do and what man receives as a benefit, so that we never stray from the true understanding of what things are and how they are — that is, of God and of man. Or did God perhaps become dissolution in us for this very reason: that, instructed through all things, we might be diligent in all things, neither ignorant of God nor of ourselves?

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological arguments regarding the incarnation, the Eucharist, and the resurrection. All scripture citations (Col 1:14, Eph 5:30, 2 Cor 12:9) are correctly identified and applied to the corresponding Latin/Greek text. The translation of 'resolutionem' as 'dissolution' (in the context of 'becoming dissolution in us') is a faithful rendering of the Latin sense in this patristic context. OCR debris and uncertain readings in the Latin (e.g., '?adyenit', '?verum', '?verum') were handled by the translators without introducing errors in the English.
